top_cited_works.title: Application of Projection-Based Reduced-Order Models to the Aerodynamic Test and Evaluation of the T-38 Aircraft
top_cited_works.abstract: Reduced-order models (ROMs) based on high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations have emerged as promising tools to streamline aerodynamic test and evaluation (T&E) of air vehicles. This study presents the development and application of projection-based ROMs (PROMs) for the T-38 Talon aircraft, aiming to accelerate flight test campaigns while maintaining predictive accuracy. This paper outlines the modeling framework, cross-code verification strategy, and flight validation results, demonstrating how PROMs can bridge high-fidelity simulations with real-world test data interpretation. Two different CFD solvers -- Stanford's AERO-F and the Department of Defense's Kestrel -- were used to compute the aerodynamic performance of the T-38. Model outputs, including aerodynamic forces, moments, and surface pressure distributions, were validated against one another and against experimental data obtained from the United States Air Force Academy (USAFA) subsonic wind tunnel. top_cited_works.title: Accelerating Flight Test and Evaluation via Aerodynamic Projection-Based Reduced-Order Models
top_cited_works.abstract: Reduced-order models (ROMs) based on high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations have emerged as promising tools to streamline aerodynamic test and evaluation of air vehicles. This study presents the development and application of projection-based ROMs (PROMs) for the T-38 Talon aircraft, aiming to accelerate flight test campaigns while maintaining predictive accuracy. Two different CFD solvers, Stanford’s AERO-F and the Department of Defense’s Kestrel, were used to compute the aerodynamic performance of the T-38. Model outputs were validated against one another and against experimental data. The AERO-F solver was then used to construct nonlinear ROMs on a four-dimensional parameter space via the least-squares Petrov–Galerkin method augmented with energy-conserving sampling and weighting hyperreduction.
